title: [Rappler Investigates] Conflict of interest
summary: Like a plague, this affliction has spread across both local and national offices, facilitated by the prevalence of political dynasties

blocks.text: It’s been a recurring theme in several stories we’ve published lately. It’s widespread, taken for granted, and its violation quite brazen among some government officials.

A conflict of interest occurs when private interests threaten to cloud or sway judgment. Public officials are discouraged from placing themselves in such a position because the temptation to exploit contracts, policies, and rulings for personal gain becomes harder to resist.
Ethics and moral principles also dictate that public officials and employees not extend favors or benefits to their relatives.
One would think the rationale is obvious: without it, government looks less like public service and more like a machine for dispensing, if not harvesting, favors.

One of our Aries Rufo Journalism fellows for 2026, Euni Barreno, with the guidance of senior editor Mia Gonzalez, reported on how public works deals involving in-laws of Caloocan City Mayor Along Malapitan raise conflict-of-interest questions.
Euni is a young, graduating journalism student at the University of the Philippines in Diliman and is a news staffer of the Philippine Collegian.
Instead of being inspired by local officials, an aspiring journalist who must report on the apparent misjudgments, if not misdeeds, of his own mayor may end up disheartened.

In his digging, Euni discovered that the recipient of multiple Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) contracts in Caloocan City, a firm named Ave-Mira Construction and Trading, is run by the in-laws of Mayor Along Malapitan.
From 2019 to 2025, according to Euni, Ave-Mira bagged 39 DPWH projects in Caloocan City worth over P731 million. During this period, Along’s father Oscar was an elected official of the city.
The Malapitans have held the mayoral post for more than a decade, with father and son taking turns after being term-limited.

Did laws on conflict of interest deter Along Malapitan and his in-laws from forging DPWH deals in Caloocan City? Apparently not. But they are not alone, unfortunately. A quick scan of recent stories yielded the following:

blocks.text: Like a plague, this affliction has spread across both local and national offices, facilitated by the prevalence of political dynasties.

Yet we are far from being deficient in laws and principles that prohibit these and frown upon conflict of interest in government. There’s the Constitution, Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards, Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, and even the Local Government Code. Too many laws but very poor enforcement.
No wonder they are regarded as mere suggestions rather than strictures for compliance. Besides, who has been fined or jailed for violating conflict of interest laws?

A profile by justice reporter Jairo Bolledo of newly-appointed Supreme Court Associate Justice Gamaliel Cordoba reminded me of the new magistrate’s ties to a commercial fishing company, Mercidar Fishing Corporation. It’s partly owned by his wife.

Was it coincidence that when Cordoba was still with the National Telecommunications Commission, the agency stopped issuing service numbers for trackers attached to fishing vessels? These trackers were intended to prevent illegal fishing within 15 kilometers of municipal waters because these are reserved exclusively for small fisherfolk.

It’s little protection for fishing boats that can’t compete with larger commercial vessels. But in 2023, a Malabon regional trial court allowed Mercidar to fish within the 15-kilometer zone. This was affirmed a year later by the High Court — of which Cordoba is now part.
What did I say about conflict of interest again? Till Thursday after next!
